before: Federated learning enables collaborative model training without centralizing raw data, and quantum machine learning offers alternative computational models for small-data classification. Whether the explanations produced by the combined system are faithful, stable, and safe to release is unexplored, and answering it first requires that federated and reference explanations be compared on a like-for-like basis. We evaluate Explainable Quantum Federated Learning (XQFL) across four quantum encodings (angle, amplitude, data re-uploading, and IQP) on the Wisconsin Breast Cancer and Pima Indians Diabetes datasets, computing Shapley-value explanations for centralized and federated models across training rounds and heterogeneous client distributions. Amplitude encoding gives the strongest two-dataset attribution fidelity (Pima IID federated-vs-centralized JSD 0.201 ± 0.101 versus re-uploading's 0.335 — the one between-encoding fidelity gap this study resolves at two standard errors, though it is no larger than the estimator's own cross-implementation noise; on Wisconsin the between-encoding differences fall within that noise). Amplitude and angle are statistically indistinguishable in round-to-round stability (Kendall's τ 0.94), both ahead of re-uploading (0.89) and IQP (0.86). Among functional runs on Wisconsin, moderate label skew (α = 0.5) shows the largest local-to-global explanation divergence while quantity skew stays close to IID; severe label skew is confounded with model collapse. Direct membership-inference AUC on the explanation vectors is highest for re-uploading (0.665) and closest to chance for angle (0.533, not resolved above chance); amplitude, IQP, and re-uploading are each resolvably above angle, and calibrated Laplace noise reduces this leakage unevenly, with no single budget bringing every encoding to near-chance. On the harder dataset, angle collapses at this circuit size while IQP is functional only under IID.

before: ESQFL [7] is the closest prior work: a digital-twin-driven, explainable, and secured quantum federated learning system for voltage stability assessment in smart grids, which uses Shapley values and differential privacy as components. The distinction from the present work is in the question each asks of the Shapley analysis. ESQFL asks which client contributed, using Shapley values for participant valuation and allocation within the federation. We ask whether a given explanation is trustworthy, decomposing that into whether the feature attribution is faithful to the federated model (RQ1), stable across rounds (RQ2), coherent between local and global models (RQ3), and safe to release (RQ4). ESQFL also applies differential privacy for security; we measure, per encoding, how much privacy budget is actually required to suppress an explanation-based membership attack.

For RQ4, each explained input $x$ carries a membership label $y_{\mathrm{mem}} = 1$ if $x$ is in the training set and $0$ if it is a held-out test point. A logistic attack classifier $g_{\mathrm{attack}}$ is fit on the standardized per-sample attribution vectors $\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}(x)$ (50 members, 50 non-members), and leakage is measured by its 5-fold stratified cross-validated ROC AUC,

$$\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{MIA}} \;=\; \operatorname{AUC}\Bigl(\bigl\{\bigl(g_{\mathrm{attack}}(\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}(x_j)),\; y_{\mathrm{mem}}^{(j)}\bigr)\bigr\}_{j=1}^{100}\Bigr). \tag{11}$$

$\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{MIA}} = 0.5$ is chance and $1.0$ is perfect member/non-member separation. As Section 7.4 discusses, this direct attack is a signal-presence proxy — it is trained and evaluated on the same target model's labelled explanations and may mildly overestimate a realistic attacker — not an exact probability of attack success. A shadow-model variant is reported alongside, and the same direct attack is repeated after noise is added to the released vectors (Section 6.5b).

### 6.5b Differential-Privacy Mechanism

The RQ4 privacy sweep adds Laplace noise to the released attribution vectors, independently per component and per released vector, and recomputes $\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{MIA}}$ (Eq. 11) on the noised vectors:

$$\tilde\phi_i \;=\; \phi_i + \eta_i, \qquad \eta_i \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathrm{Laplace}\!\left(0,\; \frac{\Delta f_{\mathrm{emp}}(\text{enc})}{\epsilon}\right), \quad i = 1,\dots,4, \qquad \Delta f_{\mathrm{emp}}(\text{enc}) \;=\; \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}_{\text{enc}}|} \sum_{(s,t) \in \mathcal{R}_{\text{enc}}} \bigl\|\boldsymbol\phi_{g,s}^{(t)}\bigr\|_2. \tag{12}$$

Here $\mathcal{R}_{\text{enc}}$ is the set of $(\text{seed}, \text{round})$ pairs with an IID, Track-A global model at round $t \ge 1$ for that encoding, and $\|\boldsymbol\phi_{g,s}^{(t)}\|_2$ is the round-logged norm of the global attribution (Section 5.1, server zone). The model is held fixed across all budgets for a given encoding–seed pair, so the sweep traces the privacy–utility curve of *explanation release*, not of a retrained private model. Evaluating (12) on the corrected sweep gives $\Delta f_{\mathrm{emp}} = 0.229$ (angle), $0.262$ (amplitude), $0.344$ (re-uploading), $0.287$ (IQP). The alternative of a conservative bound $\Delta f = 1$ (each Shapley value lies in the sigmoid range $[0, 1]$) over-suppresses: at $\epsilon = 1.0$ it drives the noise-to-signal ratio to roughly $10\times$ and $\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{MIA}}$ to $0.296$, below chance, which destroys the signal rather than calibrating against it. With $\Delta f_{\mathrm{emp}}$ the four budgets span noise-to-signal ratios from $\approx 10$–$20\times$ at $\epsilon = 0.1$ to $\approx 0.2$–$0.4\times$ at $\epsilon = 5.0$.

$\Delta f_{\mathrm{emp}}$ is a data-dependent calibration, **not a certified global sensitivity bound**: it is an observed attribution scale, not a proven bound on how far one training record can move $\boldsymbol\phi$ between neighbouring datasets. Consequently $\epsilon$ in Eq. (12) is a noise-level index that makes the perturbation comparable across encodings; the sweep does **not** establish differential privacy and **no formal $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP guarantee is claimed**. Deriving a certified sensitivity under secure aggregation is left to future work.

For RQ4, each explained input has membership label $y_{\mathrm{mem}}=1$ for a training record and $0$ for a held-out test record. Each target supplies 50 member and 50 non-member four-component Q-SHAP vectors. Both groups use the same 20-record training-derived background, disjoint from the queried member records, and the same eight-permutation estimator. This background is not an independent public reference. Standardization and logistic regression are fitted only within each outer training fold. The primary statistic is the mean of five stratified held-out fold AUCs:

$$\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{MIA}}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{h=1}^{5}\operatorname{AUC}\!\left(\{(y_{\mathrm{mem}}^{(j)},g_{-h}(\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}(x_j))) : j\in I_h\}\right). \tag{11}$$

Here $I_h$ is outer test fold $h$ and $g_{-h}$ is the attack pipeline trained without that fold. AUC 0.5 denotes chance-level ranking and 1 denotes perfect ranking, not an attack-success probability. A below-chance AUC is not evidence of privacy: reversing score direction can reveal discrimination. We additionally retain $\max(\mathrm{AUC},1-\mathrm{AUC})$ as a post-hoc orientation diagnostic, not a validated attack result. A separate direction-aware evaluation chooses score orientation and the TPR-minus-FPR threshold using four inner folds of the outer training data only. Held-out scores, labels, fold assignments and attack advantage are retained. Pooled out-of-fold TPR at low FPR is descriptive; with 50 non-members its empirical FPR resolution is 0.02. Direct MIA remains a signal-presence probe for this attack family, not a realistic attacker-success estimate or a privacy certificate. Historical shadow-model results were not re-evaluated and are excluded from current comparisons.

### 6.5b Calibrated Laplace-Noise Evaluation

Each complete set of 100 released vectors receives one independently sampled noise matrix, without reusing member noise for non-members. For a fixed target model, we evaluate the clean release and the tested noise levels $\epsilon\in\{0.1,0.5,1,5\}$:

$$\tilde\phi_i=\phi_i+\eta_i,\qquad \eta_i\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathrm{Laplace}\!\left(0,\frac{\Delta f_{\mathrm{emp}}(\mathrm{enc})}{\epsilon}\right),\quad i=1,\ldots,4,\qquad \Delta f_{\mathrm{emp}}(\mathrm{enc})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal R_{\mathrm{enc}}|}\sum_{(s,t)\in\mathcal R_{\mathrm{enc}}}\|\boldsymbol\phi_{g,s}^{(t)}\|_2. \tag{12}$$

The calibration set $\mathcal R_{\mathrm{enc}}$ contains the corrected IID Track-A global attribution logs for rounds $t\geq1$. The empirical scales are 0.229 (Angle), 0.262 (Amplitude), 0.344 (Re-uploading) and 0.287 (IQP). These are observed attribution scales, **not certified global sensitivity bounds**. Accordingly, $\epsilon$ indexes noise strength; **no formal $(\epsilon,\delta)$-DP guarantee is claimed**. Utility is the mean cosine similarity between each clean per-sample vector and its actual noisy release used by the attack, summarized across target seeds; undefined zero-norm cosines are counted rather than imputed.

An audit of the earlier release evaluation identified reused noise streams across the member/non-member groups, pooled standardization before cross-validation, and different explanation backgrounds. The corrected protocol regenerates all 115 RQ4 targets and evaluates 195 releases (115 clean and 80 noisy), with partition-integrity checks throughout. This correction replaces the earlier privacy results, including the interpretation of below-chance AUC as mitigation. It does not change the RQ1–RQ3 experiments. Because target retraining and evaluation corrections were combined, their individual contributions to the changed AUCs cannot be isolated.

### 7.4 RQ4: Privacy Leakage

At 15 seeds under IID Wisconsin, the direct membership-inference AUC (AUC_MIA, Eq. 11) is 0.533 ± 0.080 for angle, 0.620 ± 0.112 for amplitude, 0.647 ± 0.158 for IQP, and 0.665 ± 0.137 for re-uploading (Table 4, Figure 6). Amplitude (+8.7 points, 2.5 SE), IQP (+11.4 points, 2.5 SE), and re-uploading (+13.3 points, 3.2 SE) are each resolvably above angle. Measured against the 0.5 chance level, the mean AUC is resolved beyond two standard errors for amplitude (4.2 SE), IQP (3.6 SE), and re-uploading (4.7 SE), but not for angle (1.6 SE): explanation-based membership leakage is established for three of the four encodings and left at the boundary of chance for angle. The shadow-model attack fails for all four encodings (means 0.455 to 0.554): a shadow model trained without federation produces an explanation geometry that does not transfer to the federated target, so the direct attack is the appropriate one for this setting.

Two features of the direct attack qualify these AUCs. The attack classifier's feature standardization is fit on the pooled member and non-member set before cross-validation, so the absolute AUCs are a mild over-estimate; this is uniform across encodings and seeds and does not affect the cross-encoding gaps or the angle-versus-chance test. And member explanations are computed against a training-set background while non-member explanations use a test-set background, so a portion of the measured separability could reflect train/test input-distribution shift carried through the background rather than model memorization of members — angle remaining at chance bounds that portion as small. The direct-MIA AUC is therefore best read as a test for the presence of a leakage signal, not as an estimate of a realistic attacker's success.

### 7.4 RQ4: Corrected Membership-Inference and Release-Noise Evaluation

The corrected clean IID evaluation does not reproduce the earlier encoding-dependent membership-leakage ranking. Wisconsin mean direct-MIA AUCs are 0.489 ± 0.078 (Angle), 0.487 ± 0.068 (Amplitude), 0.479 ± 0.085 (Re-uploading), and 0.504 ± 0.059 (IQP), with 15 target seeds per encoding. Pima Amplitude gives 0.501 ± 0.078 at 15 seeds (Table 4, Figure 6). No IID mean is resolved above chance under the study's two-SE convention, and no between-encoding IID difference is resolved. This is an absence of detected discrimination by the evaluated attack, not evidence that explanations contain no membership information.

The IID summary retains all 15 targets, as in the original design. Wisconsin Angle and Pima Amplitude each have 14 functional targets; Track-A-only AUCs are respectively 0.490 ± 0.081 and 0.504 ± 0.080. The other IID groups contain 15/15 Track-A targets. This sensitivity analysis does not alter the qualitative conclusion. Direction selection using inner training folds also does not establish IID discrimination. Post-hoc score flipping is reported only as a diagnostic and cannot be used to select an attack on the test labels.

before: Once federated and centralized explanations are put on the same client-partition footing (Section 6.7), federated training does not by itself distort quantum model explanations under balanced client data. Under IID and quantity skew, attributions track their centralized equivalents for every encoding that produces a functional model, and round-to-round stability is high in absolute terms. The distortion that does appear is concentrated, on Wisconsin and among functional runs, under moderate label skew, and at severe label skew it is entangled with outright collapse. Amplitude encoding has the lowest two-dataset federated-vs-centralized divergence and is among the most stable across rounds (tied with angle). Releasing the explanation vectors is not free: direct membership-inference AUC is resolvably above chance for amplitude, IQP, and re-uploading (and at the boundary of chance for angle), and the noise budget needed to bring it back to near-chance depends on the encoding. A natural objection is that this fidelity result could be circular, an artifact of the federated and centralized models sharing the same low-capacity, four-feature architecture rather than evidence that federation itself preserves explanations; we test that directly with a classical control (Section 8.2).

before: Two implications follow for anyone deploying explainable quantum federated learning. First, noise calibration must be per encoding. The budget that brings angle to near-chance (ε = 1.0) leaves amplitude, re-uploading, and IQP's leakage largely intact, and bringing all four to near-chance requires a much tighter budget that also degrades explanation utility. A noise level tuned on one encoding does not transfer. Second, explanation release carries a measurable privacy cost even when the model itself is considered safe, and that cost is present across all encodings and both balanced and skewed data. Where the model is functional, quantity skew is the least disruptive non-IID condition for local-to-global divergence — Section 7.4 shows this does not extend to membership leakage — and moderate label skew is the hard case; severe label skew should be expected to remove predictive and explanatory utility together.
after: Two practical qualifications follow. First, the corrected RQ4 results do not identify an effective privacy budget or establish an encoding-dependent leakage ranking. The noise sweep measures explanation distortion, not certified privacy, and should not be used as a deployment protection rule. Second, failure of this particular attack to discriminate membership does not establish safe explanation release: stronger attacks, independent reference data and larger attack samples remain relevant. The RQ3 result is distinct: on Wisconsin, quantity skew stays close to IID in local-to-global distance, while moderate label skew is the most divergent functional condition; severe-skew comparisons remain confounded by collapse and client degeneracy.

after: **The direct membership-inference AUC is an attack-specific signal-presence probe.** Fold-local preprocessing and the common background remove two identified evaluation confounds, but the attack still uses labelled explanations from the same target and a training-derived background. before: We asked whether the explanations produced by federated quantum models can be trusted, and measured attribution fidelity, round-to-round stability, local-to-global divergence, and explanation-driven privacy leakage for four quantum encodings on two medical datasets. Answering the question required first correcting a client-to-partition assignment defect and recomputing every federated result, so that federated and centralized explanations are compared like for like. On the corrected results, federating a quantum model does not by itself degrade its feature attributions under balanced client data: under IID and quantity skew, federated attributions track their centralized equivalents and stay stable across rounds. Amplitude and re-uploading both stay functional on both datasets, and amplitude has the lower two-dataset divergence (Pima IID federated-vs-centralized JSD 0.201 ± 0.101 versus re-uploading's 0.335 — the one between-encoding fidelity difference resolved at two standard errors, though comparable in size to the estimator's own cross-implementation noise of Section 5.5, within which the Wisconsin cell-to-cell differences fall); amplitude also ties angle for the most stable attributions at 15 seeds (τ 0.94). Angle collapses on the harder dataset at this circuit size, and IQP is functional there only under IID. Releasing the explanation vectors raises direct membership-inference AUC to 0.53–0.67 across encodings at 15 seeds; amplitude, IQP, and re-uploading are resolvably above chance while angle sits at its boundary, and no single calibrated-noise budget brings all four encodings to near-chance — at ε = 1.0 angle's AUC falls to 0.415 while the others stay near 0.57, and reaching near-chance for all four requires ε = 0.1. Under severe label skew accuracy and explanation collapse together, driven by the data partition rather than by run-to-run variation. The most transferable claim is amplitude's two-dataset fidelity; the remainder is anchored to Wisconsin and should be read as such.
